title: Absence of hidden analytic conserved quantities in harmonically confined rods
authors: Sahil Kumar Singh, Abhishek Dhar, Sanjay Moudgalya
abstract: Systems of hard rods of equal length in a one-dimensional harmonic trap have been observed to exhibit peculiar non-ergodic behavior that might suggest the existence of a novel hidden conserved quantity beyond the two well known ones, i.e., the total energy and the center-of-mass energy. In this work, we investigate this possibility by systematically constraining the forms of the conserved quantities, and we rigorously rule out the existence of any extra hidden conserved quantity that is analytic in the positions and momenta of the rods involved. We do so by showing two key results: conservation during free motion demands the $U(1)$ invariance of these quantities under rotations of the position and momenta of each rod, and conservation during collisions demand an $S_N$ invariance under the permutation of the momenta of the rods as long as one of the rods have non-zero length. We then show that these conditions imply that any conserved quantity is functionally dependent on the two known conserved quantities. In addition, we show that in the special case where all rods have zero length (i.e., when they are point particles), conservation under collisions only requires invariance under a smaller $S_N$ group of permutations of the labels of the rods, which leads to a much larger set of analytic conserved quantities that we explicitly write down. In all, this rigorously clarifies the structure of conserved quantities in the hard rod problem, and motivates the application of such systematic methods to other classical systems.
summary: The paper rigorously analyzes the existence of hidden conserved quantities in hard rods confined by a harmonic trap. By imposing symmetry constraints derived from free motion and collisions, the authors demonstrate that for finite rods, only two independent conserved quantities exist. A notable exception is the point particle limit, where more integrals are found.
main_problem: The paper investigates whether a system of hard rods confined in a harmonic trap possesses hidden analytic conserved quantities beyond the known total energy and center-of-mass energy.
main_result: For general hard rods, conservation laws impose symmetry constraints ($	ext{U}(1)$ and $	ext{S}_N$) that force any conserved quantity to be functionally dependent only on the two known integrals of motion. However, for point particles (zero length), a larger set of such quantities is found.
method: The authors use systematic algebraic methods by requiring that potential conserved quantities must remain invariant under symmetries dictated by free motion ($	ext{U}(1)$) and collisions ($	ext{S}_N$).
model_or_system: The system consists of $N$ hard rods of equal length confined in a one-dimensional harmonic trap. The dynamics are analyzed for free motion, elastic collisions, and the special case where all rods are point particles.
key_observables: Conserved quantities (integrals of motion), ergodicity, and thermalization behavior.
important_parameters: Harmonic trap frequency ($\omega$), rod lengths ($a_i$), number of rods ($N$).
main_assumptions: The analysis is strictly limited to finding *analytic* conserved quantities. The comparison between finite-length rods and point particles highlights a crucial distinction in the symmetry requirements.
figures_summary: Not specified by the notes, but the text references Table 1 summarizing symmetry constraints for different dynamics (Free motion, Point particles, SMED & Rods with non-zero length).
paper_structure: The paper systematically analyzes four distinct dynamical regimes: free motion; collisions with finite rods; zero-length point particles; and Stochastic Momentum Exchange Dynamics (SMED), applying symmetry constraints in each case to determine the structure of conserved quantities.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous, systematic methodology for determining the full set of classical integrals of motion in complex interacting systems, which is foundational knowledge applicable to understanding integrability breaking in quantum many-body physics.
